analysis.one_liner: Requires owners of large fuel storage tanks to register, inspect, insure, and clean up spills.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate environment committee in March 1989, drew zero cosponsors, and never received a hearing, vote, or further action before Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created the first federal registry and safety rules for large above-ground petroleum tanks. Owners of big tanks would have had to report their age, size, and location to the states, and older, reassembled, or relocated tanks would have faced inspections, operating permits, spill reporting, and proof of insurance to pay for cleanups. It also ordered a study of the January 1988 oil spill into the Monongahela River in Pennsylvania.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near large fuel tank farms and drink water drawn from rivers and groundwater below them. The bill aimed to prevent catastrophic tank failures like the 1988 Monongahela River spill, and its financial-responsibility rules were designed so that cleanup costs and injury claims would be covered even when a tank owner went bankrupt, rather than falling on victims and taxpayers. It also required federal agencies' own tanks to meet the same rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities near large fuel tank farms

how_it_helps.text: Would require owners of above-ground petroleum tanks of 25,000 gallons or more to notify state agencies with the tank's age, size, type, and location, and would require every state to build an inventory of these tanks for the EPA — creating a public record of where large fuel stores sit.

Would direct the EPA to write spill-prevention rules for tanks that are 30 or more years old, have been reassembled, or have been moved, including inspections, operating permits, immediate reporting of releases, and cleanup requirements — the failure modes behind the 1988 Monongahela River spill.

Would require tank owners to prove financial responsibility for cleanup and for bodily injury and property damage suffered by neighbors, and would let claimants sue the guarantor directly when a tank owner is bankrupt or cannot be found.
Would cover the federal government's own tanks, letting the President grant only one-year exemptions that must be reported to Congress each January with reasons.
Would require the EPA to study the cause and environmental effects of the January 2, 1988 petroleum spill into the Monongahela River and report to Congress.

analysis.who_pays: Owners and operators of large above-ground petroleum tanks — oil companies and fuel terminal operators — who would bear notification paperwork, inspection and permit costs, cleanup liability, civil penalties up to $25,000 per day for ignoring orders, and the cost of demonstrating insurance or bonds. Guarantors and insurers would backstop claims when owners are insolvent, states would pay a 10% share of cleanup actions, and the program would be funded from the Leaking Underground Storage Tank trust fund.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil companies and fuel terminal operators

drawbacks.text: The core inspection and permit rules would apply only to tanks that are 30 or more years old, reassembled, or relocated — newer tanks would escape the safety regime — and the bill itself directs a study of whether its one-million-gallon coverage threshold should be changed, an admission the initial scope was narrow.

Compliance costs — inspections, permits, insurance, and cleanup liability — would land on petroleum storage operators and would likely be passed into fuel prices, and states would owe 10% of the cost of corrective actions.
The bill would fund its program out of the Leaking Underground Storage Tank Fund, drawing money away from the underground tank cleanups that fund was created for.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a measured, targeted response to a real hazard: large aging fuel tanks near rivers and drinking-water supplies with no federal inspection or insurance requirement. Its costs fell on a concentrated industry, and its design had real limits — the safety rules skip newer tanks and the threshold needed further study. But for communities downstream of a tank farm, the insurance and cleanup provisions addressed a genuine gap: without them, a bankrupt owner's spill becomes the public's problem.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator John Heinz of Pennsylvania introduced the bill on March 17, 1989, roughly a year after a storage tank collapse sent oil into the Monongahela River near Pittsburgh.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Environment and Public Works Committee the same day; no other senator signed on as a cosponsor.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no mark-up, no report — and the bill died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners and operators of large petroleum storage tanks, who avoided new registration, inspection, insurance, and cleanup obligations for the life of the tank fleet, and communities near those tanks gained no new protection.

for.name: Sen. John Heinz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, his response to the 1988 Monongahela River storage-tank spill in his home state, and pursued no cosponsors before it stalled.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or mark-up and never reported the bill out; the record shows no action after the March 17, 1989 referral.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, and no vote was ever taken, so the record shows no partisan split.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed registration, inspection, operating permits, spill reporting, cleanup liability, and civil penalties up to $25,000 per day on owners of large fuel tanks. Its failure left the industry without a federal above-ground tank safety regime at the time.

The bill would have required tank owners to demonstrate financial responsibility through insurance, guarantees, bonds, or self-insurance, creating a new mandated market for coverage. Guarantors would also have become directly reachable by spill victims when owners went bankrupt.
